first.rationale: The two declining metrics (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the funnel itself, and the objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue rather than a quarter of volume. Promotional pricing (memory_73) is the tempting reflex against the competitor's entry pricing, but it buys price-sensitive accounts whose revenue quality and retention are exactly what 'sustainable qualified' excludes; memory_73's summary claims 'acquisition and revenue lift' with no statement about downstream retention or margin, so it does not actually support the long-horizon objective. Referral incentives (memory_57) act on established customers and do not address a top-of-funnel/activation decay; enterprise sales assist (memory_44) is a different segment from the one being lost. So I intend simplify_onboarding, which attacks both declining metrics at their shared upstream point. I am spending verification on memory_31 and memory_86 precisely because they are the two memories my chosen action rests on, and they look suspiciously like the same finding consolidated twice (day 12 and day 52, both 'shorter signup/onboarding lifts SMB activation'). If they trace to one original experiment, my evidence base is one study, not two, and the apparent corroboration is an artifact of consolidation. I also want the original records' effect sizes, sample, and horizon: these are day-12 and day-52 findings being applied on day 76 against a market that has since changed (new competitor), and a lift measured pre-competitor may not survive the new context. Key residual uncertainty and downstream risk: memory_31 specifically credits 'cutting required fields at signup.' Removing fields can raise activation counts while degrading lead qualification, routing, and enterprise hand-off — inflating the top-line metric while lowering qualified revenue, which would be scoring against the wrong target. I therefore want the experiment run at standard scale but instrumented on qualified-pipeline and 30/90-day retention, not activation rate alone, with a guardrail that any field removed is one not used for qualification or routing. If verification shows memory_86 is merely a restatement of memory_31, or shows the original lift was small or short-horizon, I would downgrade this to a small guarded test rather than expand it.

final.rationale: Verification resolved my main worry favorably: memory_31 and memory_86 are two distinct experiments (exp_31 signup-field reduction, exp_86 onboarding-flow shortening), not one finding consolidated twice. So the corroboration is real and simplify_onboarding remains the action that touches both declining metrics at their shared upstream point. But the records also sharpen the design in a way the summaries hid. exp_86 is the stronger instrument for a long-horizon qualified-revenue objective: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention POSITIVE at +3%. exp_31 is weaker and directionally suspicious in exactly the way I flagged: signup +15% and activation +9% look impressive, but 30-day retention is -1% and qualified revenue is only +4% — i.e. most of the headline volume did not convert into durable qualified revenue. That is the signature of loosening the gate and admitting lower-intent accounts. I therefore run the exp_86 flow-shortening variant as the primary treatment and do NOT bundle in signup-field removal, since cutting qualification fields is the piece that carries the retention drag and the routing/hand-off risk to the enterprise motion (memory_44's segment). Rejected alternatives stand: promotional_pricing (memory_73) is the reflex answer to the competitor but its record says nothing about retention or margin, and buying price-sensitive volume is the failure mode the 'sustainable qualified' objective is written to exclude; referral_incentive acts on established customers and cannot fix a top-of-funnel decay; enterprise_sales_assist addresses a segment that is not the one being lost. Remaining uncertainty I am not papering over: exp_86 is a day-52 result measured before the competitor's entry pricing existed, so the effect size may not transfer to the current market, and its retention readout is only 30-day — it does not establish durability past that. exp_31 explicitly did not replicate outside SMB, which is a caution against assuming any of this generalizes. Instrumentation: score on qualified pipeline and 30/90-day retention, not completion or activation rate alone, so I do not reward a metric that can rise while value falls; guardrail that no field used for qualification or routing is removed; pre-commit to rolling back if qualified revenue per cohort is flat while completion rises.
